Subject: Nimbus <> Redwood - post-demo questions and sample schema

Thanks for the demo earlier — this was really helpful. A few follow-ups from our engineering side as we start scoping the integration: 

1) SDK + auth: which SDKs do you actively support (Node, Python, Java)? Is auth strictly API key bearer tokens, or do you support mTLS or short-lived service tokens for dedicated/private deployments? Any examples we can use to demo a secure run in our staging VPC? (We attached a small sample request schema we use for evaluation.)

2) Routing and model variants: How do you recommend routing requests for a mix of low-latency small models (for short prompts) and larger high-quality models (for long-form replies)? Can routing be per-route or per-caller and can it fallback automatically?

3) Structured output / tool-calling: We plan to use structured output (JSON responses) and a tool-calling approach for a small set of actions. Does Redwood support function/tool calling semantics that embed a typed schema in the response? How are partial / streamed tool outputs represented?

4) Embeddings and reranking: We currently use a semantic search + reranker pipeline. Does Redwood provide packaged reranker support (i.e., dense embed + light cross-encoder rerank) or should we implement reranker logic client-side? Any guidance on embedding dimensions and tokenization differences we should expect?

5) Request/response schema specifics: chat vs completions differences for our use-case (dialog state vs single-turn inference), tokenization gotchas, max_tokens enforcement, stop sequence behavior, and how streaming works (are deltas emitted as raw tokens or as JSON fragments?).

Next steps: can we schedule a 60-minute tech deep-dive next week? Our SRE and infra lead (Priya) would join.

--
Alex Grant
Head of ML Platform, Nimbus Analytics

Alex — thanks for the clear list. Great to see your engineering questions; I captured them and summarized answers below, plus next steps and artifacts we can share. Attaching a quickstart SDK guide and a high-level architecture diagram for our routing/fallback patterns.

Quick answers (high level):
- SDKs: We maintain first-class SDKs for Node and Python; Java is community-supported (example client in repo). For private/dedicated we support short-lived JWT tokens via our control plane and mTLS is available for Private on-prem installs.
- Auth: Hosted API uses API keys by default; Dedicated/Private can be configured with short-lived service tokens and KMS integration. We can provide an mTLS bootstrap guide for your staging VPC.
- Routing: Per-route routing policies are supported. You can route by route, by API key, or by tag. Automatic fallback to a compatible variant is supported (configurable thresholds).
- Tool/function-calling: We support structured function-like calls. You can declare an output schema and Redwood will return structured JSON when the model emits a matching intent. Streaming of tool results is supported as a token stream; we include framings to indicate partial structured segments.
- Embeddings/reranking: We provide managed embeddings endpoints and a lightweight reranker model you can call for top-N reordering. We also publish best-practice parameter sets for dim/normalization.
- Schema/streaming: Chat vs completions — chat preserves role/content blocks and is recommended for multi-turn stateful flows; completions are good for single-turn generation. Streaming emits token deltas; we also provide a "framed-json" mode so you can receive validated JSON fragments for structured output streaming.

Proposed next steps:
1) Tech deep-dive with your SRE + infra + app-dev folks (60m) — Marissa or Rafael to run the session.
2) Share small evaluation corpus and we’ll run an internal perf/quality pass and return suggested model profiles + cost estimates.
3) Send SDK quickstart + example routing config (attached).

When would Monday/Tuesday next week work for your team?

Regards,

Alex / Priya — hi, Marissa from the infra/serving team here. Quick technical notes to address the streaming/schema/embedding specifics so your engineers have something concrete before the deep-dive: 

1) Schema validity during streaming:
- We offer two streaming modes: token-stream (raw token deltas) and framed-json. In token-stream you receive tokens as the model emits them; you are responsible for incremental parsing and error-tolerant handling. In framed-json mode the runtime attempts to produce JSON frames (newline-delimited JSON chunks) that are syntactically valid partial objects (we include an "end_of_frame" marker). This makes partial processing safer. Example framing: 
  {"frame_index":0, "partial":"{\"action\":\"open_file\""}
  {"frame_index":1, "partial":"\", \"path\":\"/tmp/a.txt\"}"}
- For tool-calling we recommend framed-json so your orchestration can react to each tool intent as it appears.

2) Stop sequences and determinism:
- Stop sequences are enforced by the runtime before emitting tokens to the caller. In extreme failure modes (network disconnect), it is possible to see tokens that would have been suppressed, but we include an "is_final" flag in the last frame so clients can detect incomplete outputs. For critical flows, use routing to a lower-latency endpoint and enable server-side truncation rules.

3) Chat vs completions and tokenization:
- Chat: preserves roles and is better for dialog-state, streaming and tool-calling semantics. Completions: single prompt->response, fewer structured metadata features.
- Tokenization: we use an LLM-native BPE variant. You should not assume token counts identical to other vendors — always run tokenization on a sample. We publish tokenization helpers in the SDKs.
- max_tokens: configurable per-request; we enforce a hard cap per model (documented per-model). If you request a max_tokens larger than the cap, the call will fail with a 400 and an explanatory error.

4) Embeddings and reranker guidance:
- Embedding dimensions: our managed endpoint exposes 512 and 1024 dim variants; we recommend matching the variant to your existing vector store. If you migrate from another vendor expect score calibration changes — run a small AB test. Normalization: we return raw floats and suggest L2-normalize client-side if you use cosine similarity.
- Reranker: we provide a cross-encoder reranker as a managed model for top-N reorder. Typical flow: ANN search -> call embeddings for top-200 -> rerank top-20 via cross-encoder. For latency-sensitive paths use our lightweight reranker (quantized) as a compromise.

5) Practical examples (snippets):
- Chat vs completions example (Python):
  # chat (multi-turn state)
  client.chat.create(messages=[{"role":"system","content":"You are an assistant."}, {"role":"user","content":"Summarize Q1 metrics."}], max_tokens=400, stream=True)

  # completions (single-shot)
  client.completions.create(prompt="Summarize Q1 metrics.", max_tokens=400)

- Framed JSON streaming: set stream_mode='framed_json' and parse newline-delimited frames. Each frame contains metadata (frame_index, is_final).

If helpful I can paste a short framed-json parser snippet and an example rerank call ahead of the call. Otherwise Rafael or I will cover these in-depth during the session.

Cheers,
Marissa Cole
